1) AWS vs Google Cloud vs Azure

A. What services can you use for free?

Amazon Web Services (AWS) - AWS Free Tier includes a mix of “always free” services plus a free plan with credits for new accounts.  ￼

Google Cloud (GCP) - Google Cloud offers selected products free within monthly Free Tier limits, plus product-specific trials.  ￼

Microsoft Azure (Azure) - Azure provides two types of free services: some free for the first 12 months and many always-free up to monthly limits.  ￼

B. How much does it cost to run a VM for one day? (non-free plan)

Example 1: 2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM (general purpose)

| Provider | Example VM type     | On-demand $/hour | Cost for 24h   |
|---------:|----------------------|----------------:|---------------:|
| AWS      | m6i.large            | $0.096/hr       | $2.304/day     |
| Azure    | D2s v5               | $0.096/hr       | $2.304/day     |
| GCP      | n2-standard-2        | $0.0971/hr      | $2.3304/day    |

Example 2: 4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM (general purpose)

| Provider | Example VM type     | On-demand $/hour | Cost for 24h   |
|---------:|----------------------|----------------:|---------------:|
| AWS      | m6i.xlarge           | $0.192/hr       | $4.608/day     |
| Azure    | D4s v5               | $0.192/hr       | $4.608/day     |
| GCP      | n2-standard-4        | $0.1942/hr      | $4.6608/day    |
⸻

C. How much does storage cost?

To compare “object storage” across clouds (the closest apples-to-apples): AWS S3 vs Azure Blob vs Google Cloud Storage.

| Provider   | Storage product                   | Example price (per GB-month)                                                                 |
|---------:|----------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| AWS      | S3 Standard                                         | $0.023/GB-month (first 50 TB)                                                                |
| Azure    | Blob Storage Hot (pay-as-you-go example)            | ~$0.0208/GB-month (example shown in Microsoft Learn)                                         |
| GCP      | Cloud Storage Standard                              | Pricing varies by location class; see GCP pricing pages (regional/dual-region have different rates) |


D. Compare prices and expected performance of different VM offerings. Is price linear with performance?

Within the same family and generation, price is often close to linear when you scale vCPU and RAM proportionally:

	- 2 vCPU/8 GB to 4 vCPU/16 GB roughly doubles price across AWS, Azure, and GCP in the examples above.  ￼

E. Which of the three is best?

A defensible “no single best” answer (typical in coursework):

	- AWS tends to win on breadth of service and ecosystem maturity
	- Azure is often best if your company is deeply invested in Microsoft enterprise stack (AD, Windows, MS security/governance) and wants tight integration.
	- GCP is often strongest for data analytics and ML-heavy teams

F. If your company wants to start using cloud, which would you pick and why?

A solid default choice:

	- Pick AWS if you want the widest service catalog, the biggest hiring pool, and lots of reference architectures.
	- Pick Azure if you’re Microsoft-heavy (identity, security policies, Windows workloads, M365 integration).
	- Pick GCP if your early roadmap is dominated by data/ML pipelines and you want tight integration with Google’s data tooling.


2) Would cloud computing have taken off like this without virtualization?

Probably not at anything like today’s scale.

Why:

	- Virtualization (VMs, and later containers) makes multi-tenancy safe enough (isolation), enables elastic provisioning (spin up/down quickly), and allows efficient resource pooling (high utilization).
	- Without it, cloud would look more like “hosted dedicated servers” - slower to provision, harder to automate, and more expensive because providers couldn’t multiplex workloads effectively.



3-5) Armbrust et al. (2010)

1. Availability / Business Continuity - Partially true
Cloud availability improved massively (multi-zone, multi-region, managed failover), but major outages still happen and customers still need resilience design.

2. Data Lock-in - Mostly true
Containers, Kubernetes, Terraform, and open APIs reduce lock-in for basic compute, but managed services (databases, event systems, IAM, observability) still create strong lock-in - and data egress costs reinforce it.

3. Data Confidentiality and Auditability - Partially true
Security tooling is far better (encryption, KMS/HSM, IAM, logging, compliance), yet confidentiality and auditability remain central concerns, especially for regulated industries and sensitive data.

4. Data Transfer Bottlenecks - Partially true
Networks are faster, and physical transfer appliances exist, but large dataset movement, cross-region replication, and egress remain bottlenecks (cost and latency).

5. Performance Unpredictability - Partially true
Better instance isolation options exist (dedicated hosts, premium SKUs), but shared infrastructure and noisy-neighbor effects haven’t disappeared, especially for storage and multi-tenant services.

6. Scalable Storage - Mostly true
This is one area where cloud clearly delivered: object storage and managed storage systems scale elastically and are operationally simpler than most on-prem alternatives.

7. Bugs in Large Distributed Systems - Mostly true
Still a fundamental issue. Systems are bigger and more complex; the industry improved practices (SRE, chaos engineering), but distributed failure modes remain hard.

8. Scaling Quickly - Mostly true
Elasticity is real, and automation is strong (autoscaling, IaC), but organizational bottlenecks (quotas, architecture, cost controls, governance) often limit “instant scaling” in real companies.

9. Reputation Fate Sharing - Partially true
Clouds are better isolated than before, but shared dependencies still bite (shared identity providers, common SaaS outages, shared IP reputation, misconfigurations).

10. Software Licensing - Partially true
A lot moved to subscription and consumption pricing, but licensing is still messy (BYOL rules, core-based licensing, marketplace images, audit risk).
